issues.description: The study reconstructs past suicidal episodes and then analyzes archived messages, which is a retrospective case-crossover/within-person design, not a prospective design. Calling it prospective obscures the risk of recall bias, post hoc episode selection, and lack of true prediction of future attempts.
issues.quote: By reconstructing the timeline of recent suicidal behaviors through a retrospective clinical interview, we utilized a prospective research design to understand which features in text communications predicted suicide attempt

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly frames the findings as identifying or predicting imminent risk in real time, but the analyses are retrospective associations between recalled episodes and historical messages. There is no prospective deployment, no out-of-sample prediction, no calibration, and no evidence that these markers would identify future suicide attempts in real time.
issues.quote: Results suggest private electronic communication has the potential to provide real-time digital markers of suicide risk.

issues.subcategory: predictive tool claims without validation metrics
issues.description: The paper discusses development of an objective monitoring tool, but the current analyses do not estimate sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, false alarm rate, or prospective classification performance. Difference tests in a small retrospective sample cannot support claims about clinical prediction or monitoring.
issues.quote: Knowledge gained from this study could put us one step closer to the development of an objective monitoring tool capable of tracking individuals’ communication “behind the scenes,” notifying suicidal individuals and/or their clinician or family if their patterns of communication indicate increasing levels of suicide risk.

issues.description: The sample is very young, mostly female, mostly White, and largely college students. This substantially limits generalizability to men, older adults, adolescents, non-college populations, racially/ethnically diverse groups, and clinically acute populations, all of whom may differ in suicide risk processes and texting behavior.
issues.quote: Most of the participants were female, White, and college-aged.

issues.description: Participants with current high or imminent suicide risk were excluded, yet the study aims to identify imminent suicide risk. This exclusion likely removes the population most relevant for real-time clinical monitoring and may bias language patterns toward less acute or retrospectively resolved risk states.
issues.quote: Any participants with intense thoughts of suicide who were determined to be at “high risk” or “imminent risk” for suicidal behavior (as determined by a suicide risk assessment instrument) were excluded from study participation and referred for clinical care.

issues.subcategory: screening selected only a subset of attempters
issues.description: Recruitment from the participant pool required endorsing sadness/hopelessness and willingness to be contacted before being asked about suicide attempt history. This could exclude attempters whose attempts were not preceded by hopeless sadness or who were unwilling to disclose distress in a pretest, introducing selection bias.
issues.quote: On the participant pool pretest administered at the beginning of the semester (Survey 1), participants were asked, “Have you ever had a period of sadness in the past during which you felt hopeless?” and, if so, they were then asked whether they would like to be contacted about possible participation in studies that ask more questions about this period of time in their life. Those who said yes to both pretest questions were emailed a link to an additional two-question survey

issues.subcategory: broad and heterogeneous suicide attempt definition
issues.description: The primary high-risk condition combines actual/enacted attempts, interrupted attempts, aborted attempts, and subjectively endorsed planning/actions without physical enactment. These differ clinically, behaviorally, and temporally, so treating them as one 'suicide attempt episode' may dilute or distort markers of actual imminent attempt risk.
issues.quote: past actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts, using the two-week period prior to the attempt as a “suicide attempt episode”

issues.subcategory: many attempt episodes involved no physical attempt or harm
issues.description: Most analyzed attempt incidents with SMS data did not involve physical harm, and the manuscript acknowledges that some involved no enacted physical attempt. This raises concern that the 'attempt' condition does not consistently represent the construct of an actual suicide attempt or imminent lethal behavior.
issues.quote: Based on participants’ description of the objective lethality of the attempt, 29% of incidents involved some action being taken in which some physical harm was caused (e.g., taking a higher than normal dose of medication, resulting in nausea and light-headedness) while 71% of incidents did not result in any physical harm (e.g., driving to high place, such as a bridge, but deciding not to jump).

issues.description: Some 'suicide attempts' were classified based on participants’ subjective interpretation that their planning or actions were more severe than ideation. This compromises construct validity and comparability with standard definitions of suicide attempt that require self-injurious behavior with intent to die.
issues.quote: reported ‘suicide attempts’ also included incidents in which no physical attempt was enacted but in which participants considered their planning or actions to constitute a higher level of suicidal intent than ‘suicide ideation’ so they subjectively endorsed making an attempt on the screener questions.

issues.subcategory: attempt history inconsistent with ideation history
issues.description: All participants were recruited as having made an enacted, interrupted, or aborted attempt, yet lifetime suicide ideation is reported for only 90.9%. This apparent inconsistency suggests definitional ambiguity, measurement mismatch between screeners and SITBI, or possible misclassification of suicidal behavior history.
issues.quote: As expected based on recruitment criteria, all participants reported a history of at least one actual/enacted, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempt

issues.description: Episode dates and classifications were reconstructed retrospectively, sometimes for events occurring years earlier. The primary slope analyses are highly sensitive to date placement; being off by a few days can materially change estimated temporal trends in a 14-day window.
issues.quote: Participants were asked to identify a number of specific events or episodes in the past and the calendar dates during which the episodes took place.

issues.description: Although the authors report confidence in most episode dates, 'somewhat certain' dates may be off by a few days. This is consequential because the study interprets day-to-day changes immediately preceding attempts, including marginal effects near p=.05.
issues.quote: Participants were generally confident about the accuracy of the dates they selected, rating 90.3% of episodes as ‘very certain’ (i.e., exact days) or ‘somewhat certain’ (i.e., may be off by a few days).

issues.description: The experimenter interviewed participants to identify episode types and dates after recruiting them for a suicide/texting study. No blinding or independent adjudication is reported. Because episode boundaries are central to the analyses, unblinded elicitation may bias which periods are selected and how ambiguous episodes are classified.
issues.quote: participants were interviewed by the experimenter and asked to identify a number of episodes, including dates of past suicide attempts (and interrupted or aborted attempts) and two-week episodes of suicide ideation, depressive mood, and positive mood.

issues.subcategory: interview standardization and reliability not reported
issues.description: The study relies on a laboratory interview to classify episodes, but the manuscript does not report whether the interview was standardized, whether interviewers were trained, whether episode classifications were independently reviewed, or whether reliability was assessed.
issues.quote: The goal of the laboratory-based interview was to learn about past suicidal and non-suicidal events in greater detail so that digital communication made during and/or just prior to these events could later be compared using text analytic techniques.

issues.description: Attempt episodes are anchored to a suicide attempt, but ideation, depressed, and positive episodes are arbitrary two-week periods. Comparing slopes across an event-anchored window versus non-event-anchored windows is problematic because 'approaching day 0' has a clear meaning only for attempts.
issues.quote: the second set focused on testing for differences between suicide attempt episodes and other episode types, but did so by examining differences in changes in communication over time (rather than overall mean differences) between episode types.

issues.subcategory: time variable includes possible day-of-attempt leakage
issues.description: The model uses day ranging from -14 to 0 while describing the window as the two weeks prior to the attempt. If day 0 includes the attempt day, messages after or during the suicidal event could leak outcome information into the predictor window, undermining real-time prediction claims. It is also unclear whether -14 to 0 represents 15 calendar days rather than two weeks.
issues.quote: day of episode (numerical factor ranging from -14 to 0)

issues.subcategory: unclear definition of day 0 for non-attempt episodes
issues.description: For comparison episodes there is no clear event defining day 0. The manuscript does not explain how start and end dates were chosen for ideation, depressed, and positive episodes or why their temporal direction should be comparable to the pre-attempt trajectory.
issues.quote: two-week episodes of suicide ideation (not resulting in a suicide attempt); 3) two-week episodes of depressed mood or high stress (not resulting in suicide ideation or attempt); and 4) two-week episode of positive mood

issues.description: The manuscript states that the two-week window was chosen conceptually but also that the optimal window was assessed empirically by visual inspection of the same data. This introduces researcher degrees of freedom and risks capitalizing on chance, especially without preregistration.
issues.quote: The question of the optimal time window was also assessed empirically, using visual inspection of descriptive figures to identify when the rate of change appeared to be most pronounced.

issues.subcategory: visual inspection of 30-day pre/post attempt data
issues.description: Using descriptive plots of 30 days before and after attempts to decide the analytic window can introduce post hoc bias and may use information after the attempt to inform pre-attempt analyses.
issues.quote: temporal visualizations, using a smoother (loess) function, were constructed for each variable of interest and consisted of graphs plotting daily means for the given variable during the 30 days prior to and following the attempt.

issues.subcategory: large proportion of episodes lacked SMS data
issues.description: Only 134 of 293 reported episodes contained SMS data. Missingness is likely related to episode recency, device changes, phone type, and retention practices, and therefore unlikely to be missing completely at random. Mixed models do not solve biased missingness.
issues.quote: Among the episodes queried during the lab interview, 134 (46%) episodes contained SMS data, collected from 27 different participants.

issues.description: Six of 33 recruited participants did not contribute any SMS episode data, and only 15 participants had SMS data for at least one suicide attempt. This sharply reduces the effective sample for the central comparison and may bias results if data availability relates to risk history or phone behavior.
issues.quote: Among these 27 participants, 15 had data from at least one reported suicide attempt; the other 12 participants contributed data from non-suicide attempt episodes and were still included in the analyses.

issues.description: Text extraction failures due to encryption, missing old devices, unknown backups, or forgotten passwords are likely nonrandom with respect to phone type, time period, and participant characteristics. The manuscript does not quantify these failures or assess whether included and excluded episodes differ.
issues.quote: a number of iPhone users had encryption settings on their phones that prevented third-party iPhone software from accessing text data.

issues.description: The ability to recover old messages was limited, especially for older phones and cloud/laptop backups. This creates differential missingness across older versus newer episodes and may distort temporal comparisons among episode types.
issues.quote: efforts to collection additional messages outside of their current mobile device were minimally successful. Only a small number of participants brought in or had access to old phones. Also, many participants did not know whether they had laptop or cloud backups, and among those who did, a number could not remember their encryption password necessary to access iTunes/iCloud.

issues.subcategory: deleted or unavailable messages not addressed
issues.description: SMS archives may omit deleted messages, failed exports, MMS/group messages, or device-specific missing content. Because people may delete messages around crises or interpersonal conflicts, missingness could be systematically related to suicide risk, but this is not assessed.
issues.quote: all available SMS data from each device were downloaded

issues.subcategory: SMS-only analyses miss other communication channels
issues.description: The study analyzes SMS despite collecting other digital data and acknowledging migration to other platforms. If participants used Facebook, Snapchat, Gmail, or other apps differentially across time, episode type, or device era, SMS content may not represent overall private communication.
issues.quote: Additional forms of personal digital data, including phone call history, Google data (Gmail, Hangouts, and Chrome browser history), Facebook messages, and Twitter messages, were collected for the purposes of future analyses but are not part of the current study.

issues.subcategory: within-subject claim weakened by incomplete within-person data
issues.description: The design is described as within-subjects, but 12 participants contributed only non-attempt episodes and no suicide-attempt SMS data. These participants contribute to estimates of lower-risk episodes but not high-risk episodes, so key contrasts are partly between-person and vulnerable to confounding by participant differences.
issues.quote: Among these 27 participants, 15 had data from at least one reported suicide attempt; the other 12 participants contributed data from non-suicide attempt episodes and were still included in the analyses.

issues.subcategory: within-subject framing overstates actual data structure
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly emphasizes within-subject comparisons, but participants varied widely in episode availability and many did not have all episode types with SMS data. This creates an unbalanced mixed design rather than a fully within-subject design.
issues.quote: Using mixed models allowed us to account for variability among participants, episodes, and messages, leading to more accurate and generalizable population estimates for within-subject effects of episode type and resolving non-independence of the nested data. This approach also allowed us to maximize sources of variance by analyzing on the message level rather than only mean values by episode, and was especially appropriate for this dataset given the amount of ‘missing data’ (i.e., participants varied widely in terms of the number of episodes types they reported and for which they had text data).

issues.description: Although 33 participants were recruited, the central attempt analyses rely on 15 participants with attempt SMS data and 21 attempt episodes. This is very small for mixed-effects models with multiple predictors, random effects, and interaction tests, increasing both instability and Type II error while also making significant findings fragile.
issues.quote: Among these 27 participants, 15 had data from at least one reported suicide attempt

issues.subcategory: power analysis poorly matched to actual analyses
issues.description: The power analysis is based on chi-square tests and Cramer’s V, not the planned multilevel binomial/linear mixed models or interaction tests. It relies on between-subject effect sizes from different contexts and appears to assume more usable attempt data than were ultimately available.
issues.quote: We determined that a sample size of 30 suicide attempters (representing 60 attempts but only 20 with collected, usable SMS data, divided by the design effect) would provide enough power to detect only large effect sizes (Cramer’s V=0.29) for chi-square tests of mixed-effects models comparing suicide attempts to other types of episodes

issues.description: The authors tested many LIWC outcomes, two analytic families, multiple omnibus tests, and multiple follow-up contrasts, but applied no multiplicity correction. Several headline effects are marginal at p=.049 and p=.046 and may not survive correction, making false positives a serious concern.
issues.quote: Given this is a pilot study with a small and already potentially underpowered sample and the fact that we did not have concrete directional hypotheses for many of the tests, we decided not to artificially suppress Type I error (i.e., using a multiple comparisons correction)

issues.subcategory: headline effects depend on marginal uncorrected p-values
issues.description: The key findings that positive emotion and anger uniquely distinguish attempts over time include pairwise contrasts with p-values just below .05. Given the large number of tests and no correction, these effects should be interpreted as exploratory and fragile rather than reliable markers.
issues.quote: positive emotion decreased more steeply during attempt episodes compared to all other episode types, including ideation (z=1.96, p=.049)

issues.subcategory: reduced random-effects structure may inflate Type I error
issues.description: The authors planned maximal random effects but removed random slopes for day and the episode-by-day interaction because models did not converge. For within-person time interactions, omitting random slopes for time and interaction can anti-conservatively estimate fixed effects and inflate Type I error, particularly with many messages nested in few participants.
issues.quote: Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, only a by-participant slope of episode type was included in the final model.

issues.description: The manuscript describes tests as 'Likelihood-ratio (Wald chi-square) tests,' but likelihood-ratio tests and Wald chi-square tests are distinct procedures with different assumptions and test statistics. This ambiguity prevents evaluation of the reported p-values.
issues.quote: Likelihood-ratio (Wald chi-square) tests were performed to compare goodness of fit for models including and excluding the fixed effect of episode type.

issues.subcategory: p-value computation for mixed-model t tests unspecified
issues.description: For linear mixed models, p-values for t statistics depend on denominator degrees-of-freedom approximations or asymptotic assumptions. The manuscript does not specify whether Satterthwaite, Kenward-Roger, normal approximation, or another method was used.
issues.quote: Any significant tests were followed up with pairwise comparisons between each of the episode types (using z and t statistics for binary/proportion and continuous outcome variables, respectively).

issues.description: The GLMMs use binomial models for sparse word-category counts in short SMS messages, which are prone to overdispersion, zero inflation, and convergence/singularity problems. The manuscript does not report overdispersion checks, residual diagnostics, singular fits, or convergence diagnostics for final models.
issues.quote: Generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) used the “glmer” function with a logit link function appropriate for binomially distributed data

issues.subcategory: non-independence of conversations and temporal autocorrelation unmodeled
issues.description: Messages from the same conversation, recipient, or short time interval are likely autocorrelated. Random intercepts for participant, episode, and message do not account for serial dependence or recipient/conversation clustering, so standard errors may be too small.
issues.quote: Using mixed models allowed us to account for variability among participants, episodes, and messages, leading to more accurate and generalizable population estimates for within-subject effects of episode type and resolving non-independence of the nested data.

issues.subcategory: message-level analysis may inflate apparent sample size
issues.description: The study analyzes 189,478 messages, but the clinically relevant independent units are participants and episodes. Treating each message as an observation can yield very precise estimates driven by a small number of participants unless clustering and autocorrelation are fully addressed.
issues.quote: This approach also allowed us to maximize sources of variance by analyzing on the message level rather than only mean values by episode

issues.subcategory: ratios and count outcomes inadequately modeled
issues.description: Message/word counts and sent-received ratios are likely skewed, zero-inflated, and sometimes undefined when denominators are zero. The manuscript says raw continuous variables were used in LMMs but does not justify normality assumptions, transformations, or handling of zero denominators.
issues.quote: For outcome variables that were not proportion scores (e.g., number of messages sent per day), the raw continuous variable was used in a linear mixed-effects model (LMM), using the “lmer” function.

issues.subcategory: unclear unit of analysis for social-engagement models
issues.description: Social-engagement variables are described as daily counts/ratios, but the random-effects description includes a message-level random intercept. It is unclear whether analyses were at the message, day, episode, or participant-day level, which prevents replication and evaluation.
issues.quote: daily word/message counts for, and ratio between, outgoing and incoming messages

issues.subcategory: unclear whether incoming messages were analyzed as participant language
issues.description: The manuscript says each individual SMS message was scored by LIWC, but SMS archives include both outgoing and incoming messages. If incoming messages were included in self-focus or sentiment analyses, the outcomes partly measure other people’s language rather than the participant’s psychological state. If they were excluded, this needs to be stated explicitly.
issues.quote: Each individual SMS message was inputted into and scored using the 2015 version of Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC)

issues.subcategory: no handling of days without messages
issues.description: Language slopes appear to be estimated only on days/messages with text content. Days with no SMS may be informative of social withdrawal or crisis but would be missing for LIWC language outcomes, potentially biasing temporal trajectories.
issues.quote: Across all episodes, 189,478 text messages were collected and analyzed, ranging between on average about 1,200-1,600 text messages per episode.

issues.description: The manuscript reports Python cleaning but omits important details: handling of emojis/emoticons, URLs, abbreviations, autocorrect, spelling errors, non-English messages, group texts, MMS, duplicate backups, automated texts, and message direction. These decisions can materially affect LIWC scores.
issues.quote: participants’ SMS data files were individually cleaned using Python to standardize the encoding of messages and naming of variables across all participants.

issues.subcategory: LIWC single-word categories weak for informal SMS sentiment
issues.description: LIWC dictionary counts may not capture meaning in short, informal text messages because negation, sarcasm, slang, context, emojis, and multi-word expressions are often crucial. This threatens construct validity of sentiment and self-focus measures.
issues.quote: One weakness of this approach is that examining single words in isolation can fail to capture the semantic context of the word (e.g., “not happy” would count as “positive emotion” because negation is not accounted for)

issues.description: The interpersonal theory constructs are thwarted belongingness and perceived burdensomeness, but the study operationalizes social engagement using counts and ratios of incoming/outgoing messages. These metrics do not directly measure support, belongingness, rejection, burdensomeness, or relationship quality.
issues.quote: we tested whether suicide attempters demonstrated greater signs of disengagement from and burdensomeness on their social support networks prior to suicide attempts compared to other episodes by examining patterns in outgoing vs. incoming messages.

issues.description: A lower sent-to-received ratio could indicate disengagement, but it could also indicate receiving support; a higher ratio could indicate help-seeking or distress rather than engagement. The operationalization does not uniquely map onto the intended construct.
issues.quote: decreased social engagement (i.e., lower ratio of sent vs. received text messages).

issues.description: Depressed mood or high stress episodes among people with attempt histories may still represent elevated suicide risk, even if participants did not report ideation or attempt. Labeling them 'minimal/no risk' may misclassify risk levels and obscure gradients.
issues.quote: depressed and positive episodes were considered “minimal/no risk.”

issues.description: Changes in anger or positive emotion may reflect life events that precipitated both texting changes and suicidal crises, such as breakups, exams, job stress, family conflict, treatment changes, or substance use. The models do not adjust for such episode-level confounds, so markers may not be suicide-specific.
issues.quote: Participants were then asked to describe specific details of and context surrounding each time period.

issues.description: Participants varied in diagnoses, treatment, medication, and mental health history, but these variables were only used descriptively. Differences across episodes or participants could confound language patterns, especially given incomplete within-person data.
issues.quote: Participants also reported on current and past treatment experience (e.g., medications, therapy) and psychiatric diagnoses.

issues.description: The paper states that variables were selected a priori and presents hypotheses, but also describes many exploratory elements and does not report preregistration of outcomes, model specifications, time windows, exclusion rules, or multiplicity strategy. This increases concern about undisclosed analytic flexibility.
issues.quote: Numerous aspects of this research were exploratory by nature.

issues.description: Participants could report up to three episodes per type, but the manuscript does not specify how episodes were selected when more than three existed, whether most recent, most severe, most memorable, or participant-chosen episodes were used. This creates selection bias and limits replicability.
issues.quote: For each episode type, we asked about a maximum of three episodes (e.g., three suicide attempts if participant has three or more lifetime attempts).

issues.description: The manuscript does not report whether episode windows could overlap or how overlapping windows were handled. Overlap between ideation, depressed, positive, or attempt windows would contaminate condition comparisons and violate independence assumptions.
issues.quote: A total of 3 to 12 episodes were collected for each participant depending on the presence and number of reported events.

issues.subcategory: effect sizes and uncertainty inadequately reported
issues.description: The tables provide model coefficients for some contrasts but no confidence intervals, odds ratios, predicted probabilities, or absolute LIWC category rates. This makes it difficult to judge clinical or practical magnitude, especially for statistically significant but tiny log-odds slopes.
issues.quote: Here, β (standardized values of the model parameter estimates in log odds units) are reported and serve as effect sizes.

issues.description: The manuscript describes β as 'standardized values' in log-odds units, but the table values appear to be unstandardized logit coefficients and no standardization procedure is described. This creates ambiguity in interpretation and effect-size reporting.
issues.quote: β (standardized values of the model parameter estimates in log odds units) are reported and serve as effect sizes.

issues.subcategory: discussion claims anxiety effect not supported by results
issues.description: The discussion states that attempts were associated with greater anxiety and sadness in mean analyses, but the reported omnibus test for anxiety was nonsignificant and the Results section says no significant anxiety effect emerged.
issues.quote: In terms of overall mean differences, few reliable differences emerged though results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness.

issues.description: The Results state that desire to die decreased from pre to post, but Table 1 reports a positive change of 0.20. This discrepancy creates ambiguity about score direction or calculation of change.
issues.quote: desire to die from pre (M=0.82, SD=1.10) to post (M=0.61, SD=0.90) significantly decreased slightly, t(32)=2.23, p=.033.

issues.description: The risk assessment section refers to negative mood and desire to die, then later to a 'desire to hurt self question.' It is unclear whether the same item, a different self-harm item, or a suicide-specific item was used for safety decisions.
issues.quote: score greater than 3 on desire to hurt self question

issues.subcategory: omnibus table labels and statistics incomplete
issues.description: Tables report statistics as '2=...' rather than clearly identifying χ², and Table 2 has duplicated or malformed column headers. This impairs clarity about test statistics and degrees of freedom.

issues.subcategory: language coverage and non-English texts not reported
issues.description: LIWC is dictionary-based and language-specific, but the manuscript does not state whether all messages were in English, how non-English texts were handled, or whether LIWC coverage differed across participants or episodes.
issues.quote: LIWC searches a text file and calculates normalized word counts for nearly 6,400 words, word stems, and emoticons

issues.description: The manuscript refers to private text communication habits as 'digital biomarkers.' These are behavioral/language features inferred from communication, not validated biomarkers, and no biological or diagnostic validation is provided. The terminology may overstate construct status and clinical readiness.
issues.quote: potentially provide clues into the suicidal mind and may serve as temporally sensitive markers of suicide risk.

issues.description: Private SMS data are naturalistic, but they are still self-presentational communications shaped by audience, concealment, relationship context, and deliberate impression management. The manuscript overstates resistance to bias.
issues.quote: Private digital communication... provides ecologically valid data that accumulates automatically and is thus resistant to biases common to the research process, such as demand characteristics or efforts at impression management.

issues.description: The within-attempter design is useful for proximal comparisons but cannot determine whether identified patterns are unique to suicide attempters versus broader distress or typical texting variation in non-attempters. This limits interpretation of markers as suicide-specific.
issues.quote: By comparing multiple periods of high vs. low suicide risk, all within a sample of suicide attempters

issues.subcategory: nonfatal attempters may not generalize to suicide deaths
issues.description: The study necessarily includes only nonfatal attempters and acknowledges that suicide completers may differ. Claims about preventing suicide deaths or identifying those at imminent lethal risk should be tempered.
issues.quote: It is possible that characteristics of suicide attempters differ from those of suicide completers

issues.subcategory: episode types may differ systematically in recency
issues.description: Because SMS availability depends on device history and participants retrospectively selected episodes, attempt, ideation, depressed, and positive episodes may differ in recency. Language style, platform use, social networks, and age change over time, confounding episode-type effects.
issues.quote: availability of and access to personal messaging data dating back prior to significant life events (e.g., suicide attempt)

issues.description: The primary interaction models assume a linear day-to-day trend across the episode window. The manuscript itself notes that changes were variable and often concentrated around seven days prior, suggesting nonlinearity. Linear slopes may miss or mischaracterize acute changes.
issues.quote: Although highly variable across variables, changes tended to occur most notably and often around 7 days prior to the suicide attempt.

issues.subcategory: no matched control periods within the same calendar context
issues.description: The design does not report matching comparison episodes to attempt episodes on day of week, season, academic calendar, relationship status, treatment status, or phone/device era. Texting language is plausibly affected by these contextual variables.
issues.quote: two-week episodes of suicide ideation, depressive mood, and positive mood
